answers.explanation: TCP/IP doesn't care what's underneath. Any network that can carry a packet can join.
Keeping acknowledgments at the ends lets the network in the middle stay simple.
Both sides speak the same published protocol (SMTP, for mail), so it doesn't matter who wrote each program.
Every host gets an address, and routers carry packets between networks to get there.
The IETF is an open community of engineers. Anyone can join a working group's mailing list.
The name dates from 1969, when they really were requests for feedback. Today RFCs include the Internet's official standards.
An RFC is never changed after publication. A later RFC updates or replaces it. TCP's original RFC 793 was replaced by RFC 9293 in 2022.
Broad agreement in the working group, backed by implementations that actually work.
Working documents are Internet-Drafts. Once a working group agrees, a draft can be published as an RFC on the standards track.
